subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO FURTHER LEGISLATION TO BE BROUGHT DOWN
speechtext: Now that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) has brought down his budget I should1 like to ask the Prime Minister if he is in a position to indicate to the house whether we now have before us all the legislation that will be introduced this session with the exception of what may arise out of the resolutions now before the committee of ways and means and anything that may oome from other committees of the house. I should like to ask also whether the government intends to proceed at this session with the redistribution measure and if there is any possible way in which that measure might be expedited.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO FURTHER LEGISLATION TO BE BROUGHT DOWN
speechtext: The shipping bill now in the other chamber will be proceeded with and the pensions bill will be brought down. The redistribution bill will be proceeded with, and I think every reasonable effort is being made to expedite the work of that committee, at least that is my advice in that regard. Amendments to some existing statutes probably will have to be brought down, affecting possibly the Post Office Act, the Public Works Act, the Judges Act and the criminal code. Owing to the great difference of opinion that has been expressed by different public bodies with respect to the proposed legislation arising out of the Gibb report I am not in a position at the moment to say whether or not that bill will be proceeded with. It has been printed, but a great many public bodies in the cities affected have been directing communications to the government suggesting that the matter be delayed until they can further consider it. At the moment I cannot say whether or not. we will proceed with that measure at this session. I think two or three other statutes, the names of which I do not recall at the moment, will have to be amended as well. I will endeavour to indicate clearly on Monday, so far as one may do so with certainty, the legislation that will be proceeded with.

Mr. Chairman, I have taken a good dead of interest in this question ever since I had the honour of becoming a member of this house. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) this afternoon gave a resume of some resolutions submitted to the Department of Labour over a period of ten years. I would like to give a resume of what action this house has taken in regard to this question of unemployment insurance.
Early in 1926 a communication was sent to the then leader of the opposition as well as to the hon. gentleman who led the government at the time. It dealt with the question of unemployment insurance as well as old age pensions, and requested their views on those very important subjects, dealing, that is, with the temporary question of providing for the unemployed at the time and also the question of unemployment insurance. Some action was taken toy the government in providing relief for the unemployed for the winter of 1926-27, and when the session of 1927 came around a motion was introduced by myself asking that the matter of unemployment insurance be referred to a committee, I think of the house. But it did not pass in that session. A similar resolution was adopted in 1928 and referred to the committee on industrial and international relations, where the question was gone into veiy thoroughly. During that session, however, we did not have sufficient time to' bring in a complete report, which later was done, approving in a general wiay of the principle of unemployment insurance but pointing out the constitutional difficulties standing in the way. In 1929 I do not think much action was taken, though I believe the question was raised, and in 1930 we were in much the same position. Then came the election of 1930, and unemployment insurance was discussed from many platforms in all parts of the country. The principle was accepted by both major parties; both agreed on the principle of unemployment insurance and both were prepared to do something if they were returned to office. In the early part of the session of 1931 I again raised the question, and the right hon. Prime Minister gave a definite understanding that within the lifetime of the present parliament legislation would be introduced looking towards 'the establishment of a system of unemployment insurance.
It is quite true, as the Minister of Labour has said, that a great many things have taken place since that time, and conditions have become greatly aggravated. I am very anxious indeed, even at this late date, to see a start made on some form of unemployment insur-

ance, but it is a question whether legislation of that kind would even begin to remedy our troubles. The Minister of Labour has said that approximately a million and a third men, women and children, are on relief in Canada to-day, and when I say that there are at least eight hundred thousand people out of work the committee will have some idea of the problem we are facing. If we are to hold out any hope for those men and women out of work I feel that at least they should know the actual conditions. If we should have a scheme of unemployment insurance inaugurated at this time, I think even an optimist of the highest order would have to admit that it could affect only an extremely small proportion of those who find themselves out of work at present. I believe we have out of work roughly one-third of those usually gainfully employed, and from a financial standpoint, under the existing economic system I think lit would be almost impossible to provide in anything like a reasonable way for those people. So if we are to deal with the unemployment problem in such a way as to provide reasonable relief I think vre should attack the problem in a more fundamental way than merely by considering the question of unemployment insurance.
I should not like to be misunderstood, Mr. Chairman. I am heartily in favour of unemployment insurance even at this time, but at the same time I think we should look at the problem in a far more practical way than merely the consideration of this one method of dealing with it. I think we should realize that of the hundreds of thousands of people unemployed to-day a great percentage never will be reabsorbed into industry. That being so the question becomes far more important than the provision of a scheme of unemployment insurance. The man or woman out of work cannot possibly contribute to any insurance scheme, and those who are employed only on part time scarcely could be expected to do so. With the federal and provincial exchequers in a depleted condition and with the condition of industry generally it would be almost impossible to provide the vast sums that would be necessary to bring into operation any scheme of unemployment insurance that would be actually sound, so we must look in another direction for ways and means of providing work for those of our people who are unemployed to-day. In my opinion -there is only one thing to do, and that is to provide work. I am bitterly opposed to the dole; I detest the very thought that in this country we have a million and a third of our people receiving public relief, and even

Reliej Act, 1933
that does not tell the whole story. In addition to this vast number there are many others who are receiving private relief, and I venture to assert that if all those in receipt of relief from other than public sources were added to the total I have mentioned we would have about a million and a half people receiving relief to-day. In other words, at least one out of every seven of our population is in receipt of some form of relief.
As I said a moment ago, Mr. Chairman, the logical thing to do is to provide employment. Public works have been ruled out of the picture because they are too expensive. I quite agree, because the amount of work provided by the expenditure of $15,000,000 or $20,000,000 by the federal government would only touch the fringe of the unemployment situation. During the past few years our army of unemployed has been growing greater and greater, and in spite of the optimism displayed by certain hon. members of the house I see no betterment at the present time. When I picked up the paper this morning I found that action was being taken by our railways which will have the effect in the near future of throwing thousands more of our working people out of employment, thus greatly aggravating an already difficult situation. So with all due respect to what has been done by the government in the last few years; with all due respect to those who even at this time advocate unemployment insurance which, at the best, is only a palliative and will not affect a very large proportion of those out of employment, I think if we are to deal with this question at all we must do so from a different angle altogether. The one way I see, and the method I have advocated in this house for a number of years, is to first reduce the number of hours of work so that we may absorb into industry large numbers of those who are now idle. To me that is the first remedy that should be applied. I know I will be told that the question of the hours of labour is under the jurisdiction of our provincial authorities. To a certain extent this may be quite true, but I believe that when the need is so great; when in our large industrial centres throughout the country we have a third of the employable population out of work, we should not balk at the constitution. I believe in having all respect for the constitution, but the need is urgent now, and I think our provincial authorities should be big enough to consider the welfare of the country as a whole and do something fundamental to deal with this ever-increasing problem of unemployment.
We are told that we are faced with conditions such as never have been known in the Dominion of Canada before. That is perfectly true. In common with the rest of the world we are faced with a serious economic crisis, but that crisis is man-made, and such a crisis we should meet ourselves; we ought to be able to overcome it by proper action taken in this house. The vast army of the unemployed in Canada to-day are looking to this parliament for redress, because this is the only body in the country they can look to for some relief. There is nothing more demoralizing to a man than to be out of work and to be without any prospect whatever of obtaining work either immediately or in the near future.
As a first step towards solving the unemployment problem, I suggest that some means must be taken by this house of considerably reducing the hours of labour in industry. But there is something else that must go along with that, because merely to reduce hours of labour and at the same time to reduce wages would leave us in relatively the same position we are in now. The next essential therefore is to provide purchasing power for the masses of the people so that they may consume the goods which they themselves help to produce. At present that purchasing power is lacking and consequently there is no effective demand for the goods which we have in superabundance.
I know that the solution cannot be found by any of the provinces; it would be unfair to ask any of the provinces to take the necessary steps towards a reduction of the hours of labour. There is only one body competent to legislate along that line and that is this honourable house. If we take these two steps which I suggest we shall have a complete change from the present situation in industry. Industry to-day operates not in order to serve the community as a whole but to serve the ends of those who own and control it, and industry must be made to realize that it exists to serve a much higher purpose than that. It must serve the needs of the community. There could be nothing more striking in the way of condemnation of our present industrial system than the spectacle of 800,000 people walking the streets unemployed and without any prospect of obtaining employment, while at the same time our factories are idle, although these very people are ready to start the wheels of industry going. And these people are in want of the very things the factories can turn out if they are given a chance to function.
Relief Act, 1933

This problem can be solved only by reducing very considerably the hours of labour, and secondly, by increasing the purchasing power of the great masses of the people. I do not attach much importance to conferences. Some hon. gentlemen who have preceded me have emphasized the last conference and others of the same kind, but personally I must say that I have lost a good deal of faith in any sort of conference, and so have the people. What the people are looking for is action, and they expect this house to take that action. I believe that the government itself is anxious to do something for the unemployed. It would be a splendid thing if the government could see its way clear, by proper action, to reduce the army of unemployed whom it is compelled to maintain, and I suggest that if we are to deal with the problem this government can deal with it in one possible way only, and that is by considerably reducing the hours of labour. If that were done we could absorb men and women into industry and start things going. And secondly, I repeat, we must increase the purchasing power of the masses of the people so that they may be able to obtain in large measure the goods which they themselves produce.

speechtext: As the department over which I have at the moment the honour of presiding is and has been for some time looking into this question of unemployment insurance, may I say a word in regard to the matter. I believe the experience of other countries would indicate that that is far from the truth. Since 1911 there has been an unemployment insurance scheme in Great Britain, and to-day unemployment in that country is as great a problem as it is here. True, unemployment insurance is a more scientific way of dealing with the difficulty than the method we are adopting, but it certainly is not a solution. If we had the best possible scheme of unemployment insurance we would still have an unemployment problem to solve.

In the last four sessions, including the special session of 1930, we have been discussing unemployment. When that special session was called the Prime Minister asked for an appropriation similar to the amount mentioned in the amendment to this resolution, such moneys to take care of the situation then obtaining. In that special session he pointed out that a special vote of money was not a solution of the difficulty, but merely a palliative. Again at this time, after the passage of three years, nothing but a palliative is offered. It seems to me that if we are to deal effectively with the unemployment problem we will have to do something of a more permanent character.
The condition with which we are faced is this: Every employing company, every industry, is trying to produce the greatest number of units of commodities with the least possible amount of labour time. With such conditions confronting us it is impossible under the present plan to catch up with the unemployment problem. We cannot do it, and for that reason, while, as the hon. member for North Winnipeg suggested, we might consider unemployment insurance as a means to an end, I suggest we must remember that unemployment insurance is not an end in itself, but that we must have a more fundamental and definite plan to deal with unemployment.

The minister was quite right this afternoon when he said that when and if we establish an unemployment insurance scheme it must be on a sound actuarial basis. I say that we cannot be on a sound actuarial basis until in Canada we have a sound money system. I do not mean by that the present system, because it is anything but sound. It

Relief Act, 1933
is sound, but very little more, to most people. Sound money would be stable money. When stable money is put to work properly it will bring about stable conditions, stable employment and stable purchasing power. When we have such conditions it may be possible to bring in an unemployment insurance scheme which would be actuariailly sound. Had an unemployment insurance scheme been introduced and put into operation in 1928 or 1929 I am afraid by .this time it would have failed, because there would not have been enough income in the hands of those administering the fund to pay the unemployment insurance. All that goes back to the fact that we have not a sound money system. We should have a money system whereby money issued has some reasonable relation to the amount of goods produced. Under such conditions we would not have all this unemployment. Until we deal with our money system we will have unemployment, and I am afraid we will have more than obtains to-day.
I was glad to hear the Minister of Finance announce yesterday that a royal commission will be appointed to inquire into banking and money. I hope one of the matters with which the commission will be specifically charged to inquire into will be the control of our money system so as to maintain stable employment in Canada. We can produce the goods but we have yet to solve the problem of distribution. That is the reason we have unemployment. I again suggest to the committee that before we can effectively deal with unemployment, we must deal on a scientific basis with the money problem.

speechtext:
I wish to bring to the attention of the minister the position that many municipalities find themselves in. We agree that governments to-day, both dominion and provincial, are carrying a heavy load in regard to unemployment. But so are the municipalities. I believe I am safe in saying that the municipalities to-day are carrying a heavier load than the provincial or the dominion governments. They are further crippled by the fact that municipalities have not the powers of taxation that the other governments have. In the province of British Columbia the municipalities for many years past have been in receipt of large grants from the provincial government. Now the provincial government, in an endeavour to balance its budget, has intimated to the municipalities that some of these grants will be cut off. A grant which has been given them in connection with the parimutuel and the liquor profits, amounting to some $640,000 is going to be cut off this year. In view of that condition there are
three questions that I would like to ask the minister:
In the event of any municipality being unable to carry on financially will the Dominion government contribute a greater proportion than one-third to direct relief?
In the event that it does, will it be on the understanding that the province will bear one-half instead of one-third as at present?
If the province finds itself unable to bear the fifty per cent, or any further burden in connection with the municipalities, will the Dominion government bear a greater proportion, say two-thirds?
I feel sure that many municipalities are going to be seriously crippled by having these grants taken from them this year, so it is very important that these questions be answered. Many municipalities have gone into bankruptcy or receivership already, and many more will do so this year owing to the cutting off of these grants.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: The three overlapping questions asked by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) will have to be dealt with when the conditions arise. I do not want to keep reiterating what has been said so many times in recent years as to where the primary responsibility lies for taking care of those unable to take care of themselves. If it comes to pass that individuals are unable to provide for their own needs, and the municipalities and the province of British Columbia find themselves at the end of their resources, then we would have to review the situation at once and with care to see what the difficulties were. But this government does not intend to project itself into an investigation of the municipalities of British Columbia or any other province. If there is danger of the situation developing there that has been suggested, this government, in so far as it can assist, will have to wait and deal with the matter when it arises.

speechtext: I have just one further question to ask the minister. We are being asked to vote $20,000,000 for direct relief; in other words, so far as the government has a policy it is a policy of the dole, and in that respect the limit is placed at $20,000,000.

It is direct
relief, simply giving money for relief purposes and not providing work. I distinguish between direct relief, in the form of money given

people who require add, and money spent in order to return people to the land, putting the landless man on the manless land as someone has said, or the construction of public works or matters of that kind. Under this measure the government is asking for a blank cheque so that, apart from what is required for the purpose of the dole, they will have an unlimited amount available for the relief of unemployment in other ways. The minister has told us that in the last two years, during which the government has had this blank cheque, they have spent or loaned a total of something like $115,000,000. As I pointed out the other day that sum is equivalent to the total expenditure of Canada for one year in the period immediately preceding the war, and I suppose this year the expenditure will be proportionately the same.
I want to ask the minister whether, apart from the dole for the expenditures that may be made under this blank cheque, he has any comprehensive, constructive, coordinated plan which he can announce to this house as that of the ministry for dealing with the question of unemployment relief.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
It is so easy for an hon.
member to rise in his place and talk about great big coordinated schemes; that word is a very euphonious way of describing almost anything. Let me point out that as far back as the years 1921, 1922 and 1923 and from 1926 on, as revealed in the files of the Department of Labour, the leader of the opposition himself recognized the difficulties that confront any dominion government in this country with respect to taking over the administration of relief for those in distress or those who are unable to look after themselves-difficulties in relation to provincial and dominion jurisdiction respectively. This government will pursue the same course as it has pursued during the past year. That is to say, the moneys will be devoted first to assisting the provinces where they are unable to take care of their own worthy needy people, and will assist the provinces in projecting any schemes or plans which they may conceive or which we may conceive and which will be Satisfactory to them or to us, as the case may be, within the financial limits of the provinces and the dominion, to provide employment or to take care by way of direct relief of those who are in need.
What the future has in store for us I am not going to prophesy. I believe that the situation is certainly not getting any worse, in spite of what people say. I know there are certain people who would be gratified indeed to have their own prophecies come 
true and to see things become worse. There is that sort of mind. There are people who, having prophesied, desire to see their prophecy fulfilled, no matter what hardship may befall anyone.
The Dominion government will not invade the jurisdiction of the provinces. I hazard the opinion that, set up in every municipality in Canada, there is some commission or organization that is taking care of immediate needs and directing the efforts that are being made in this regard. Even when times are normal, when there is no financial distress, when business is as usual, there is not a municipality in this country that has not its indigents, persons who have had some misadventure and cannot geit along. These agencies are extended and are working throughout Canada to supply those who are in need during this time.
I assume that the leader of the opposition had in mind a big cooperative national committee which this government should set up to take the place of all these various agencies in the municipalities and the various charitable organizations throughout Canada, and to take over the whole matter as a dominion effort. With that point of view I am not in agreement, not only because of the question of jurisdiction, but because there are many, many associations in Canada to-day, as there have been in the past year, who have devoted their time and money towards the aid and succor of those in distress. One of the reasons for not embarking on such a scheme as is suggested is that, in my view at any rate, these wells of charity will very soon dry up because unfortunately there is ingrained in the human makeup a desire perhaps to shift responsibility.
We will continue to do as we have done in the past year, and in spite of the criticisms that have been made as to the reduction in the amount of money that has been devoted to direct relief, I still say that this government and the provinces and municipalities are to-be commended for having introduced system into the giving of direct relief throughout Canada, as well as in view of the fact that the cost, while perhaps the numbers have increased as they always have done in winter months in this country, is very materially reduced.
I hope that with the return of even a little better times and with the attention that is being paid towards sytematizing direct relief, the cost this year will be still less. I do not think any government can successfully ask. commeudation simply because it has spent huge sums of money on any project without

regard to the efficiency of the organization that is spending the money, and without regard to the beneficial effect of such expenditure. This government, I say, will pursue the same course as it pursued last year, and if eventualities arise where some change in some section of Canada becomes necessary, the government will take such appropriate action as may be deemed desirable.

speechtext:
The minister seems to take exception to my words because they suggest a nationwide scheme, and he says he assumes that I had in mind what has been proposed from this side as a national commission that would co-operate with the provinces and municipalities in an endeavour to deal with this great problem of unemployment relief. What I had in mind was what the government announced in the speech from the throne on March 12, 1931, as the policy which it intended to put into effect. On that date the speech from the throne made this announcement:
The operation of The Unemployment Relief Act, 1930, has proved equally beneficial. While the grant authorized by this act could not immediately have checked unemployment arising from causes of which you have full knowledge, yet its careful administration by my ministers, ably aided by the provincial and municipal governments and the two great railway systems, has resulted in the institution of a nation-wide program of public undertakings, each one a unit in a scheme of national development, which have collectively provided work for the greatest number of men who have ever been employed through the direct efforts of the federal government.
That was the announcement of the government's policy-a great national scheme of development as a means of helping to solve the problem of unemployment-and to-day the minister tells us that to speak of a nationwide scheme is only to try to introduce something that will embarrass the whole situation. I just want to make clear to him that the government did begin by announcing its intention to deal with -the problem in a nationwide fashion in order to help to solve the problem, but it has thrown that policy to the winds and the only policy it now has is that of the dole. It is not in a position at the moment to announce anything in the shape of a comprehensive, coordinated, constructive plan of dealing with this great problem.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
With reference to the
observations of the right hon. gentleman, at the time of which he speaks there was a plan that contemplated the projection and anticipation of public works that were contributed to by this government, by the provinces, by the municipalities and by the railway systems, and which ran into huge figures. The soundness of that plan could perhaps be measured, in a way at least, by the duratior of this depression, because it was obvious then, as it is now looking back, that such schemes could not be projected year after year. But it was carried on as the speech from the throne then indicated it would be. In my judgment all that the state-by state I mean the municipalities, the provinces and the dominion-can afford to do is to take care of those who for any cause are unable to take caTe of themselves. Suggestions have been made that we should build a factory here or a warehouse there, the claim being made that the amount granted to such a project would soon be eaten up in the granting of direct relief where nothing would be left to show for the money expended. The fact is that the money spent upon the erection of a factory, a dock or something else would employ perhaps only fifty or one hundred people upon a wage basis whereas the same money expended in direct relief would provide food, fuel, clothing and shelter to perhaps ten times that number of people and for a longer period of time.
